usage: There is a thing / I have something
There are a lot of things
examples: 이 물건은 뭐예요?
What is this thing?
Pointing at an unknown physical object
가방에 물건이 너무 많아요.
There are too many things in the bag.
에 marks the container; 물건이 많다 = lots of stuff
손님, 이 물건은 환불이 안 돼요.
Sir/Ma'am, this item can't be refunded.
Shop register: 물건 = the merchandise itself
nuance: 물건 is the Sino-Korean 物件 (物 'thing' + 件 'item/case'), the catch-all word for a tangible, hold-in-your-hand object when you don't know or don't need its specific name, and in a store it shifts to mean the merchandise/goods. The sharp contrast is with 것 (and its spoken form 거): 것 is a grammatical 'thing' that can stand for anything at all, even abstractions or whole situations (좋은 것 = a good thing/one), whereas 물건 is strictly a concrete physical item you could pick up — you would never call an idea, a plan, or a feeling a 물건. It is neutral in register and safe with anyone. Common collocations: 물건을 사다/팔다 (buy/sell goods), 물건이 좋다 (the goods are good quality), 물건을 고르다 (pick out an item). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 물건 every time you'd say 'thing' in English; for 'I have a lot of things to do' you need 일 (work/matter), not 물건, and to count items you say 물건 다섯 개, never '다섯 물건'.

mistakes: Saying 할 물건이 많아요 for 'I have many things to do' — 물건 is only physical objects, so this must be 할 일이 많아요 (using 일 = task/matter).
Using 물건 as a counter, e.g. 한 물건 — 물건 is a noun, not a measure word, so count with 개: 물건 한 개, 물건 두 개.
Calling an abstract 'thing' like a good idea 좋은 물건 — for non-physical 'things' use 것: 좋은 것이에요 (it's a good thing).

examples: 상자 안에 뭐가 있어요?
What's inside the box?
안에 = inside; asking about contents
이 상자는 너무 무거워서 못 들겠어요.
This box is too heavy, I can't lift it.
-아서 gives the reason; 들다 = lift
택배 상자를 칼로 뜯었어요.
I cut open the delivery box with a knife.
택배 = parcel; 뜯다 = rip/tear open
nuance: 상자 is the Sino-Korean 箱子 (箱 'box/chest' + the noun-forming 子), the standard word for a rigid box or carton — cardboard moving boxes, gift boxes, shipping cartons. Its everyday rival is the loanword 박스 (from English 'box'); the two overlap heavily and a Korean might say 박스 하나 just as readily, but 상자 sounds a touch more proper/written while 박스 is breezier and dominates for things like a 'case' of bottled water (생수 한 박스). Contrast it with the soft containers it is NOT: 봉투 (a flat envelope or paper bag) and 봉지 (a flimsy plastic/paper sack) collapse and have no rigid walls. Count boxes with the generic 개 (상자 한 개) or, for full-box quantities, the loan counter 박스. The pitfall for English speakers is reaching for 상자 for a tiny rigid case — a jewelry or glasses case is usually 케이스 or 갑, not 상자.

mistakes: Calling a plastic shopping bag a 상자 — a bag that collapses is 봉지 (plastic) or 봉투 (paper/envelope); 상자 has rigid walls.

Opening a sealed cardboard box with 열다 only — 열다 works for a lid, but to slit packing tape you naturally say 뜯다 (tear/cut open): 상자를 뜯다.

examples: 종이 한 장만 주세요.
Just give me one sheet of paper, please.
장 counts flat sheets; 만 = just/only
여기 종이에 이름하고 전화번호를 써 주세요.
Please write your name and phone number on this paper here.
종이에 = onto the paper, filling a form
프린터에 종이가 다 떨어졌어요.
The printer is out of paper.
다 떨어지다 = run out completely
nuance: 종이 is a pure native Korean word for paper, both as the material (made from 나무/pulp) and as a sheet of it. The crucial point is its counter: flat, thin things are counted with 장 (종이 한 장, 두 장) — the same 장 used for tickets (표 한 장), photos (사진 한 장), and pizza slices, so learning 종이 anchors the whole 'flat-sheet' counter family. Distinguish the raw material 종이 from finished paper products that have their own names: a 신문 (newspaper), a 책 (book), a 공책/노트 (notebook), and a filled-out 서류 (document) are all made of 종이 but are never just called 종이. Useful collocations: 종이에 쓰다/적다 (write on paper), 종이를 접다 (fold paper), 종이를 자르다/찢다 (cut/tear paper). The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: defaulting to 개 instead of 장 to count sheets, and using 종이 for a form you must complete — that is 서류 (paperwork) or the document's specific name.

Writing 'on paper' with the wrong particle, e.g. 종이를 써요 for 'write on paper' — use the surface particle 에: 종이에 써요 (종이를 쓰다 would mean 'use up paper').

usage: Please give me a plastic bag
I put it in a plastic bag
Do you have a plastic bag?
examples: 비닐봉지 하나만 주세요.
Just one plastic bag, please.
At a convenience store checkout
과일이 무거우니까 비닐봉지에 따로 넣어 주세요.
The fruit is heavy, so please put it in a separate plastic bag.
-니까 gives the reason for a request
요즘은 마트에서 비닐봉지를 안 줘요.
These days marts don't give out plastic bags.
Reflects Korea's plastic-bag restrictions
nuance: 비닐봉지 stitches together 비닐 (from English 'vinyl', here meaning thin plastic film) + 봉지 (a flimsy sack/pouch), i.e. the thin film bag you get at shops and markets. In fast casual speech Koreans clip it hard — to just 봉지 ('봉지 드려요?' = shall I give you a bag?) or even 비닐 ('비닐 주세요'). The contrast to nail down is the container family: 비닐봉지/봉지 is thin and flimsy, 봉투 is a paper bag or an envelope, and 가방 is a sturdy reusable bag/backpack you own. Because Korean stores charge for bags and supermarkets have largely stopped offering single-use ones, 비닐봉지 주세요 / 봉투 필요하세요? are bread-and-butter checkout lines. The big pitfall is the word 비닐 itself: it does NOT mean English 'vinyl' as in vinyl records (that's LP/레코드) or vinyl flooring siding — in Korean 비닐 just means cheap plastic sheeting/film. Also don't pluralize or count it oddly: 비닐봉지 한 장 (counted with 장, like other thin flat things) or 한 개 both work.

Saying 비닐봉지에 담아요 vs 넣어요 interchangeably for small items — for dropping items in you usually say 넣다 (put in); 담다 implies loading/filling a container and suits baskets or boxes better.

usage: I put it in the basket
examples: 과일을 바구니에 담으세요.
Please put the fruit in the basket.
담다 = load/put into an open container
빨래 바구니가 벌써 가득 찼어요.
The laundry basket is already full.
가득 차다 = be full to the brim
장바구니에 담아 두고 나중에 결제했어요.
I added it to the cart and paid later.
장바구니 = shopping cart, online or in-store
nuance: 바구니 is a native Korean word for a basket — an open-topped container, often with handles, that you carry or fill: a market basket, a laundry basket, a fruit basket. It is highly productive in compounds, and two are essential: 빨래 바구니 (laundry basket) and especially 장바구니, which means both the traditional grocery/shopping basket AND the 'cart' on an online store (장 = market shopping + 바구니). The verb that goes with it is 담다 — to load/put things into an open vessel — which is exactly the contrast to remember: you 담다 into a 바구니 (open) but you might 넣다 (insert) into a closed 상자 or 봉지. Distinguish 바구니 (open, often woven or plastic, hand-carried) from 상자 (a closed rigid box) and from 카트 (a wheeled trolley/cart): the hand basket you pick up at a mart is a 바구니, the big push-cart is a 카트. Count them with 개 (바구니 두 개). Pitfall: English 'shopping cart' maps to 카트 for the wheeled one but to 장바구니 for the website 'cart' — don't say 카트 for an online basket.

Saying 카트 for an online shopping cart — Korean websites use 장바구니 ('add to 장바구니'), not 카트.

usage: I fill the bucket with water
examples: 양동이에 물 좀 받아 오세요.
Please go fill the bucket with water.
물을 받다 = collect/run water into
양동이가 물로 가득 차서 무거워요.
The bucket is full of water, so it's heavy.
-아서 = and so; reason + result
비가 새서 양동이를 받쳐 놨어요.
The roof leaks, so I set a bucket under it.
받쳐 놓다 = place underneath to catch
nuance: 양동이 is a bucket or pail — a deep, usually handled vessel for carrying or holding water, typical of cleaning and chores. It is one indivisible native word: do NOT split it into 양 + 동이. In real daily speech you will constantly hear the casual substitutes 통 (a generic tub/canister — 물통, 쓰레기통) and the older loanword 바께쓰 (from Japanese-via-Dutch 'bucket'), but 양동이 is the clean standard form to learn and say. The verbs that pair with water-into-bucket are 담다 (put/load in) and 받다 (catch/collect running water): 양동이에 물을 받다. Contrast it with smaller open vessels: a 그릇 is a bowl/dish for food, a 대야 is the wide shallow basin you wash your face or feet in, and a 양동이 is the tall bucket for hauling water. Pitfall: English 'a bucket of X' tempts a 의 ('of'), but Korean simply juxtaposes — 물 한 양동이 (one bucket of water), counting with the noun itself.

Confusing 양동이 (deep water bucket) with 대야 (wide shallow washbasin) or 그릇 (food bowl) — pick by shape and use, not size alone.

examples: 이 깡통 좀 따 주세요.
Please open this can for me.
따다 = pop/open a can or bottle
빈 깡통은 캔으로 분리해서 버리세요.
Throw empty cans in the can recycling, separated out.
분리하다 = sort/separate for recycling
깡통 안에 옛날 동전이 가득 들어 있었어요.
The tin was full of old coins.
들어 있다 = be (contained) inside
nuance: 깡통 is a metal can or tin — a food tin, a paint can, an old biscuit tin. The verb to open it is 따다 (to pop/pull open), the very same verb used for opening a bottle or popping a drink can, which is the key collocation to lock in: 깡통을 따다, 병을 따다, 캔을 따다. Here is the register/usage split learners miss: for a beverage can specifically (soda, beer, coffee), Koreans overwhelmingly say the loanword 캔 — 콜라 캔, 맥주 한 캔, 음료수 캔 — and 캔 is also the recycling category, while 깡통 leans toward food/industrial tins and can carry a slightly humble or old-timey flavor (깡통차 = a beat-up old car). So 캔 and 깡통 overlap but aren't identical: order a drink and it's a 캔; describe a dented food tin and it's a 깡통. Count both with 개 or 캔 (콜라 두 캔). Pitfall: opening a can with 열다 sounds off — 열다 is for doors, lids, and books; a sealed can is 따다.

usage: I lock it (put the lock on)
examples: 사물함에 자물쇠를 채웠어요.
I put a lock on the locker.
채우다 = fasten/lock on; 사물함 = locker
자물쇠 열쇠를 잃어버려서 못 열어요.
I lost the key to the lock, so I can't open it.
열쇠 = key; -아서 = and so
창고 문은 항상 자물쇠로 잠가 두세요.
Always keep the storeroom door locked with a padlock.
잠그다 = to lock; -아 두다 = keep (in a state)
nuance: 자물쇠 is the physical lock device itself — a padlock or hasp lock — the native-Korean counterpart that forms a matched pair with 열쇠 (key): the 자물쇠 is what you lock, the 열쇠 is what opens it. Notice the shared 쇠 ('metal/iron') in both words, a nice memory hook that they're two halves of one metal pair. Mind the verbs, because Korean splits 'lock' across several: 잠그다 is the all-purpose verb 'to lock' (문을 잠그다 = lock the door); 채우다 is 'to fasten/put a lock on' something (자물쇠를 채우다); and to unlock you say 풀다 (undo) or 열다 (open). Contrast 자물쇠 with the modern keypad/smart lock on apartment doors, which Koreans call 도어록 or 번호키, not 자물쇠 — 자물쇠 evokes a key-and-shackle padlock. Pitfall: English 'lock' is both noun and verb, but in Korean the object 자물쇠 cannot be verbed — you can't '자물쇠 something'; you 자물쇠를 채우다 or simply 잠그다.

examples: 문 손잡이를 돌려서 여세요.
Turn the door handle and open it.
돌리다 = turn (something); -아서 chains the actions
흔들리니까 손잡이를 꼭 잡으세요.
Hold on tight to the handle, it's shaky.
Bus/subway announcement style; 꼭 잡다 = grip firmly
쇼핑백 손잡이가 무게 때문에 끊어졌어요.
The shopping bag's handle snapped from the weight.
끊어지다 = snap off; 때문에 = because of
nuance: 손잡이 is a transparent native compound — 손 (hand) + 잡이 (a holder/gripping part, from 잡다 'to grasp') — literally 'the hand-grab', i.e. any handle, knob, grip, or hold you take hold of: a door handle, a drawer knob, a mug's handle, a kettle grip, the strap/rail you hang onto in a bus or subway. Because it's built from 잡다, the natural partner verb is 잡다 (hold/grab) — 손잡이를 잡다 — and for a turning knob, 돌리다 (turn): 손잡이를 돌리다. It is extremely productive in compounds: 문 손잡이 (door handle), 컵 손잡이 (cup handle), 가방 손잡이 (bag handle), so you rarely need a separate word per object. Two contrasts help: 손잡이 is the grip you hold, whereas 자물쇠/도어록 is the lock mechanism, and 버튼 is a press-button — different parts of the same door. Pitfall: don't reach for 들다 ('lift the whole object') when you only mean grabbing the grip; you 잡다 a 손잡이. Also, the strap you hold standing on the subway is exactly 손잡이, not a borrowed English word.

examples: 신발 끈이 풀렸어요.
Your shoelace came undone.
풀리다 = come untied (intransitive)
가방 끈이 너무 길어서 줄였어요.
The bag strap was too long, so I shortened it.
끈 = strap here; -아서 = and so
택배 상자를 끈으로 단단히 묶었어요.
I tied the parcel box up tightly with string.
끈으로 = with string (수단 'means'); 단단히 = firmly
nuance: 끈 is a one-syllable native word (note the double-consonant ㄲ onset and the ㄴ batchim) covering flexible string, cord, strap, or lace — anything you tie or carry with: shoelaces (신발 끈), bag straps (가방 끈), apron ties (앞치마 끈), a drawstring (끈). It sits in the middle of a thickness scale that learners should sort out: 실 is fine sewing thread, 끈 is a string/cord/strap you bind and fasten with, and 줄 is a thicker line/rope (and 줄 also means a 'line/queue' of people). Its bread-and-butter verbs are 묶다 (tie/bind) and 풀다 (untie/loosen), with 풀리다 as the 'comes undone by itself' intransitive. Useful collocations: 끈을 매다 (tie/do up a lace), 끈을 조이다 (tighten a cord), 끈을 묶다/풀다. Pitfall: English uses 'tie' for shoelaces, but watch the active/passive split — you 끈을 묶다 (you tie it), yet when it loosens on its own you say 끈이 풀렸다 (it came untied), not 끈을 풀었다 (which means you deliberately untied it).

examples: 바늘에 실 좀 꿰어 주세요.
Could you thread the needle for me?
꿰다 = pass thread through; 좀 softens the request
바늘이 너무 뾰족해서 조심해야 돼요.
The needle is very sharp, so you have to be careful.
뾰족하다 = pointy; -아서 = and so
시계의 긴 바늘이 12를 가리켜요.
The clock's long hand points to 12.
바늘 = clock hand; 가리키다 = point at
nuance: 바늘 is a native word for a needle — the thin, sharp implement used with 실 (thread) for sewing; 바늘과 실 (needle and thread) is a set phrase, like English. Crucially, 바늘 stretches by metaphor to two other 'needle-shaped' things English keeps separate: the hands of a clock (시계 바늘 — the 긴 바늘 minute hand, 짧은 바늘 hour hand) and a hypodermic needle (주삿바늘), so the one Korean word spans sewing needle, clock hand, and syringe. The verb you must pair correctly is 꿰다 — to pass thread through the eye — 바늘에 실을 꿰다 (thread is threaded into the needle, marked with 에). Because it's sharp, it collocates with 뾰족하다 (pointy) and 찌르다 (prick/stab): 바늘에 찔리다 (get pricked by a needle). Pitfall: don't use 묶다 (tie) for threading — you 꿰다 the thread through; and English 'thread the needle' inverts the Korean direction, where the needle takes the 에 particle (into the needle) and the thread is the object.

examples: 바늘하고 실 있어요?
Do you have a needle and thread?
하고 = and (casual); asking to borrow
실이 자꾸 엉켜서 짜증나요.
The thread keeps getting tangled, it's annoying.
엉키다 = get tangled; 자꾸 = repeatedly
빨간 실 한 가닥으로 단추를 달았어요.
I sewed the button on with a single strand of red thread.
한 가닥 = one strand; 달다 = sew/attach on
nuance: 실 is the native word for thread or yarn — the fine strand used for sewing and knitting, the lifelong partner of 바늘 in the set phrase 바늘과 실. The single most useful fact is its dedicated counter: a strand of thread is counted with 가닥 (실 한 가닥, 두 가닥), the same 가닥 used for a strand of hair (머리카락 한 가닥), so 실 teaches you a counter, not just a word. Sort it firmly from its thicker cousins: 실 is fine thread/yarn, 끈 is a string/cord/strap for tying, and 줄 is a rope or line — a gradient from thinnest to thickest. Natural collocations: 실을 꿰다 (thread it through a needle), 실이 엉키다/풀리다 (the thread tangles/unravels), 실이 끊어지다 (the thread snaps), and the compound 실타래 (a skein of yarn). Two pitfalls: first, don't borrow 끈 for sewing thread — that's too thick. Second, beware the homophone trap — the syllable 실 also appears as a Sino-Korean prefix 實 'real/actual' (실시간 'real-time', 실제 'actual') and as 室 'room' (교실 'classroom'); as a free-standing noun, though, 실 means 'thread'.

examples: 단추를 끝까지 채우세요.
Button it up all the way.
채우다 = fasten; 끝까지 = to the very end
더우니까 맨 위 단추 하나만 풀었어요.
It was hot, so I undid just the top button.
풀다 = unbutton; -니까 = since
셔츠 단추가 떨어져서 다시 달아야 돼요.
A shirt button came off, so I have to sew it back on.
떨어지다 = fall off; 달다 = sew on
nuance: 단추 is specifically a clothing button — the disc you fasten on a shirt, blouse, or coat. The verbs are a tidy set worth memorizing together: 채우다 (or 잠그다) to button up, 풀다 to unbutton, and 달다 to sew a button on (with 떨어지다 for one falling off). The contrast that trips up every English speaker is 단추 vs 버튼: English uses 'button' for both clothing fasteners AND press-buttons on machines, but Korean splits them — a button on a remote, elevator, keyboard, or website is 버튼 (loanword), reserved for the press kind, while 단추 is strictly the sew-on clothing kind. So you press the 버튼 on the 엘리베이터 but fasten the 단추 on your 셔츠. (There is also the idiom 첫 단추를 잘못 끼우다 — 'fasten the first button wrong' = get off on the wrong foot, where buttoning is 끼우다.) Pitfall: never say 단추 for a device button (that's 버튼), and don't use 묶다 (tie) to button — buttons are 채우다/잠그다, not tied.

examples: 비가 와요. 우산 있어요?
It's raining. Do you have an umbrella?
Everyday rainy-day check-in
우산을 안 가져와서 비를 다 맞았어요.
I didn't bring an umbrella, so I got soaked.
비를 맞다 = get rained on; -아서 = and so
우산을 지하철에 놓고 내렸어요.
I left my umbrella on the subway (and got off).
놓고 내리다 = leave behind on getting off
nuance: 우산 is Sino-Korean 雨傘, literally 雨 'rain' + 傘 'umbrella/parasol' — so the word transparently means 'rain-umbrella', which is your built-in reminder it's for rain. The verb is the deceptively busy 쓰다: to put up/use an umbrella is 우산을 쓰다, the same 쓰다 that covers wearing a hat (모자를 쓰다) and glasses (안경을 쓰다) — Korean groups 'things over your head/face' under 쓰다, distinct from 입다 (clothes on the torso/legs) and 신다 (footwear). The contrast to file away is 우산 vs 양산: both are 傘, but 우산 (雨傘) is the rain umbrella while 양산 (陽傘, 'sun-shade') is a parasol against sunlight — different words for different weather. Useful collocations: 우산을 쓰다/접다/펴다 (put up / fold / open an umbrella), 우산을 챙기다 (remember to grab an umbrella), 우산을 깜빡하다 (forget the umbrella). A folding umbrella is 접는 우산 or 3단 우산, a long one 장우산. Pitfall: English 'wear/carry an umbrella' must become 쓰다 (use over the head), never 입다, and don't reuse 우산 for a sun parasol — that's 양산.
